title: Role-specific GTM talk tracks: ML engineers vs backend vs platform teams
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working draft of short, role-targeted talk tracks and objection-handling for sales, AE enablement, and partner engineers. Focus: how to frame Redwood Inference to three adjacent engineering personas (ML engineers, backend engineers, platform teams) so messaging is concise, technical, and operationally useful.

Notes on tone and constraints:
- Keep it technical but pragmatic: persona cares about measurable outcomes (latency, cost, reliability, dev time).
- Use comparative framing vs building in-house and vs managed endpoint competitors.
- Include 1–2 quick proof points (numbers, features) per persona.
- Include short email/opening lines and one-call objectives.

Structure of this doc (quick nav):
1) One-liners and elevator pitches per persona
2) Core pain points and how Redwood solves them (bulleted)
3) Objections + scripted counters
4) Competitive traps and differentiation cues
5) Sample outreach lines and one-call agenda
6) Open questions / TODOs for GTM collateral

1) One-liners / elevator pitches
- ML Engineer: "Ship model-driven features faster with predictable inference economics — Redwood gives you model versioning, quantization-aware runtimes, and rollout controls so you can iterate models without blowing your infra budget."
- Backend Engineer: "Integrate a single, stable inference API that matches your latency SLOs and scales with traffic — Redwood handles batching, smart routing, and fallbacks so your app stays fast during spikes."
- Platform Team: "Standardize inference across teams with policy-driven routing, private deployment options, and observability that ties cost to token-level traces — reduce variance in unit costs and unlock centralized controls."

2) Core pain points + Redwood framing (short)
ML engineers (what they say): slow iteration loops to production, model regression surprises, fragility when changing quantization or sequence lengths.
How Redwood answers:
- Model lifecycle + rollouts: version pinning, canary, A/B rollout and auto-fallback for quality regressions.
- Quantization-aware runtime: recommendations + tested kernels to avoid silent quality drops.
- Eval hooks & CI integration: push-time evals and regression alerts so you know if performance changed.
Proof point idea: "Reduced model rollout incidents by X% in internal pilot" (replace X with pilot metric).

Backend engineers (what they say): unpredictable latency and token cost, complexity of deploying GPUs, and request spikes that blow tail latency.
How Redwood answers:
- Smart routing + latency tiering: route to compatible variants or regional capacity to meet SLOs.
- Automatic batching with latency floors: continuous batching that respects per-request latency constraints.
- Out-of-the-box L7 API + SDKs: REST/SDK that mirrors existing request-response patterns, no custom gRPC rewrite.
Proof point idea: "Median P95 tail latency stable under 3x traffic in stress tests."

Platform teams (what they say): inconsistent inference patterns across teams, lack of cost visibility, governance/compliance requirements.
How Redwood answers:
- Centralized controls: per-tenant policies, region controls, and private deployments (VPC/on-prem).
- Cost attribution + token-level traces: tie model, route, and token spend to owners.
- SLA & dedicated pools: reserved capacity with predictable throughput and contractual SLAs.
Proof point idea: "Customer X reduced unit cost variance across org by Y% after standardizing on Redwood."

3) Common objections and suggested counters (scripted)
Objection A: "We already have an inference infra team; we can build this ourselves."
- Counter: "Totally fair — you can build many pieces, but two things are hard to keep competitive: the continuous kernel/runtime tuning across architectures and commercial-grade rollouts tied to cost SLOs. Redwood is optimized for both and reduces operational toil so your infra team can focus on product differentiation, not constant kernel tuning or caching heuristics. Do you have metrics on how much time your infra team spends on kernel/sequence tuning per model?"

Objection B: "We need full data sovereignty / on-prem — can you run inside our network?"
- Counter: "Yes — Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packages with customer-managed networking and KMS/HSM integrations. Most customers start in hosted for speed and move select workloads private for compliance. If you share your primary compliance needs we can map a path (hosted -> dedicated -> private) and timeline."

Objection C: "Cost — the hosted API looks expensive compared to raw GPU instances."
- Counter: "Compare unit economics, not raw instance cost: Redwood yields lower per-token cost via continuous batching, prefix caching, and model selection routing that chooses cheaper compatible variants under load. We can run a pilot on a representative workload and show a 90-day cost projection vs your current baseline."

4) Competitive traps and differentiation cues (callouts for reps)
- Trap: Competitor sells single "super-low latency" numbers without specifying workload shape (seq len, batch, cold cache).
  Cue: Ask about their workload distribution and whether the benchmark used short sequences and no KV cache. Position Redwood's runtime as workload-aware with KV/prefix cache.
- Trap: Vendors emphasize model breadth alone.
  Cue: Reframe to ask about SLOs: "How do they handle rollouts, failover, and per-tenant isolation at scale?"
- Trap: DIY pitch from infra teams: they assume future cost will drop enough to justify building.
  Cue: Emphasize ongoing maintenance (kernel updates, quantization regressions, ops runbook) and offer a 30–60 day pilot to validate operational savings.

5) Sample outreach lines and one-call agenda
Cold email subject lines:
- "Cut per-token costs on LLM features without re-architecting"
- "Reduce inference incidents during traffic spikes — quick question"

Short opening for demo/intro call (30–45 minutes):
- 0–5m: Introductions + customer context question (current models, SLOs, infra ownership)
- 5–12m: Pain calibration (ask about recent incidents, rollout pain, cost opacity)
- 12–25m: Show 2 slides: Runtime architecture (how bundling batching/caching works) + quick console view (cost + latency traces)
- 25–35m: Pose proposal: 30–60 day pilot on representative route; success metrics: P95 latency within target, cost delta vs baseline, no model regressions during rollout
- 35–40m: Next steps (stakeholders, data access, pilot kickoff owners)

Role-specific quick scripts (for AE/SE to memorize)
- ML engineer opener: "Tell me about model churn — how often are you deploying new weights or quantized variants? I want to hear where your current pipeline breaks down."
- Backend opener: "What SLOs do you care about (p50/p95/p99) and at what traffic ranges? Where are you seeing tail spikes today?"
- Platform opener: "Which teams are using inference today and how do you chargeback/measure unit costs? Are policy controls (region, model whitelist) a blocker to consolidation?"

6) Open questions / TODOs
- Get internal pilot metrics to replace X/Y placeholders (ask eng for recent rollout incident counts and a small customer cost delta example).
- Ask product for 1–2 canonical benchmark reports showing P95 under both short and long seq distributions.
- Create a 1-page battlecard vs top 3 competitors (emphasize runtime + rollouts + private options).
- Draft a short technical FAQ for SEs: kernel selection, KV cache behavior, quantization-induced regressions.

Informal notes / scratchpad (for internal use)
- Slack refs: #g2m-product-feedback, #solutions-eng — loop Samir for pilot scoping.
- Quick win idea: ship a short playbook for pilot customers that maps sample payloads -> expected savings calculation.
- Unresolved: We should standardize the "pilot success metric" names (cost_delta_pct, latency_p95_ratio) so legal/commercial can bake into SOW templates.

End of draft — purposefully concise. Aim to iterate this into a 1-page persona cheat sheet + a 3-slide SE pitch.
